features.title: Path variables
features.summary: A route path can hold a path variable, such as `{id}` in `GetRoute("/{id}")`. A path variable is a part of the URL that can change, such as an ID. `FromPath` puts its value into the method parameter with the same name. The parameter type is checked first. When `id` is a number, `/items/abc` gets 400. On the Tac side, a page folder whose name starts with an underscore, such as `client/pages/items/_id/`, matches any value. The view passes `page.path` to a service method, which reads the last segment. So every service language can use the value: a service in a language other than JavaScript or TypeScript has no DOM, but its methods take arguments from the view.

features.title: Shared data and the page
features.summary: A view (the HTML template of a page or component) reads `client/shared/data/<name>.json` as `data.<name>`. It reads the path of its document as `page.path`. It reads whether it runs in development mode as `page.development`. No service (a class that holds the state and behavior of a view) is needed (ADR 0036). Put content that has no behavior in these data files, not in a service. If the file is missing, the build fails with `TY1311`. No service may use `data` or `page` as its instance name.

features.title: Service classes
features.summary: A service is a class that holds the state and behavior of a view. A view refers to a service by its instance name: `BasketService` is `basket`. `{basket.count}` reads a field, and `on:click="basket.add()"` calls a method. Fields hold the state of the view. Methods give its behavior. By default, a service is a page singleton (one shared instance for the whole page). Every component that names it shares that one instance. `NeedsAll` creates one service instance for each component instance. It uses the properties of that component. `Lifetime({"value":"prototype"})` also gives other services one instance for each component. `OnStart` runs after injection (the framework gives the service the objects it needs). It also waits until the component is attached to the DOM (the tree of elements on the page). `OnStop` cleans up work that the service owns. A declared `applicationEventPublisher` field and `OnEvent` replace local publish and subscribe code that you would write by hand. A `Needs` field named after a browser resource receives that resource. There is no general framework object on the instance. Ordinary imports and helper functions still work. Constants are static class fields.

files.name: conventions
files.code:
Service                         one class per client/services/<Name>Service file
Lifetime({"value":"prototype"}) one instance per component instead of per page
OnStart                         initialized owner and DOM
OnStop                          owned cleanup
applicationEventPublisher       declared field; publishEvent(model[, retain])
OnEvent({replay,condition,id})  listener for the model type of its parameter
Order(n) / InBackground         listener order; detached delivery
Needs <name>                    view, lifecycle, cacheManager, resourceLoader,
                                taskScheduler, applicationEventPublisher
Needs / Named("Name")           injected field; named provider when it differs
$field / $$field                per-tab / cross-session persisted state

Spring has the same ideas: Service, Scope, lifecycle, ApplicationEventPublisher
and named resources, through Jakarta annotations. Tachyon uses plain English
names for them (ADR 0047). The browser resource contracts are Tachyon-specific.
Remote Yon topics/SSE remain a separate explicit API.

features.title: Shared behavior annotations
features.summary: Tac and Yon share these annotations across their supported languages. The role, injection and description annotations are `Service`, `Helper`, `HTTPClient`, `Store`, `Converter`, `Setup`, `Lifetime`, `Needs`, `Named` and `Description`. Injection means the framework gives a class the objects it needs. The caching, data and resilience annotations are `CacheSettings`, `Cached`, `UpdateCache`, `ClearCache`, `PageDefaults`, `Retry`, `MaxAtOnce`, `AllOrNothing`, `Entity`, `Id`, `Table` and `Query`. `HTTP request annotations`, `Convert` and `Schedule` cover outgoing HTTP calls, mapping values and scheduling. The configuration annotations are `Settings`, `WhenProfile`, `WhenSetting` and `Setting`. The validation annotations are `Checked`, `Check`, `Required`, `NotEmpty`, `Length`, `Min` and `Max`. The test annotations are `Test`, `TestSetup`, `UseProfiles`, `TestSettings`, `Fake`, `FreshStart` and `ValueSource`, and a test case checks its result with `Assert`. Write each marker (annotation) on its own line. Marker options use strict JSON. The compiler turns the markers into runtime code inside the same source file. It does not use a reflection scanner (code that inspects classes while the program runs). The markers are global, so no language needs to import them. Native services use typed adapters with no embedded JavaScript. Tac stays client-only, and Yon stays REST-only. Each adapter has one clear owner. Queries have limits and must be authorized. The cache changes only after a call succeeds. Data transfer object (DTO) validation is pure: it has no side effects. Configuration keys start with the prefix of their realm: `TAC_` or `tac.` for Tac, and `YON_` or `yon.` for Yon. You give this configuration yourself. Markers with no arguments can be written without parentheses, as in Spring: `@Service`, `@Setup`, `@Needs`, `@Converter`. A plain `@Service` can be a Tac role or a Yon role. The folder that holds the file decides which one (ADR 0038). The service below needs no network or storage adapter. Role types must be in plural folders, and their file names must match their type names exactly. Collaborators are classes that a service works with. Tac finds annotated collaborators in the same language under `client/services`, `client/stores`, `client/clients`, `client/setups`, `client/entities`, `client/helpers` and `client/converters`. Yon uses matching folders under `server/`. Only controllers are placed next to their route. `Test` units go in `server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext>` or `client/tests/<Name>Test.<ext>`, and `ty test` runs them. On managed Yon roles, `Needs` finds the provider for each marked field. So you do not need to write a constructor by hand. `Named` chooses a provider when the field name does not identify it. Tac types and unmanaged types still set up their behavior contexts themselves.

Each service receives an explicit behaviors context. Derive its partition

Structured queries additionally require authorizeEntity(command, execution).
Entity adapters own parameterized operations.
HTTP adapters honor redirect: 'error', credentials: 'omit', cancellation,
deadlines and the bounded response while reading. Never bundle server
credentials in Tac. No annotation adds SSR or native capabilities.

Behaviors.construct(Type, values) for generated constructors.

decorators cannot rewrite inferred method or constructor signatures.

files.name: bounded query and cache policies
files.code:
Store(Entity, {fields, defaultSize, maxSize}) is a contract with no
implementation, like a Spring Data repository interface. A Store without
an Entity is refused (TY1308). Referenced Entity/Table and query classes
use exact role filenames in their realm's shared role folder. Methods
without a body become find/count/exists commands; derived
findByStatus/countByStatus/existsByStatus are supported.
Predicates combine with AND; no SQL, OR, joins or arbitrary expressions.
authorizeEntity(command, execution) must return true before adapter execute.
Find is bounded to page size <=100 with annotation-owned ordering and
an ID tie-breaker. Caller page.sort must be empty. Results stay bounded JSON.

UpdateCache/ClearCache({method: 'find'}) target a same-class Cached method
and match its key parameters by name. Its page input and key policy are reused. Authorization
and key/adapter checks precede mutation; store/delete follows successful
bounded output and lifetime checks. Put never reads. No atomic database/cache
transaction, automatic reconciliation, retry or AllOrNothing is promised.
Annotation object options must be written as strict JSON.

files.name: configuration and validation boundaries
files.code:
Settings binds explicit nested tac/yon snapshots into typed JSON.
Each underscore in prefixed names maps to a path segment; no ambient environment access.
Unknown selected-prefix keys fail. Setting binds one field by path from the parsed application configuration
through Behaviors.values; Tac may name only tac.*, Yon only yon.*.
WhenProfile/WhenSetting inspect
snapshotted explicit inputs before configure. Never ship server secrets to Tac.

Checked marks direct DTO fields. Required/NotEmpty require values;
Length counts UTF-8 string bytes or array/object entries. Min/Max accept finite
numbers without coercion. Length/Min/Max otherwise ignore missing/null.
Check validates the selected method argument before pagination/cache/HTTP/body.
Behaviors.validate(Type, value) needs no context or DTO construction.
Errors expose redacted field/rule paths. Unknown fields remain allowed.
No nested groups or automatic field assignment; validate again in Yon.

features.title: Caching public reads
features.summary: The manifest's `tac.cache` declares service-worker policies for public reads, grouped by path. A service worker is a browser script that can answer requests from a cache. features.title: REST controllers
features.summary: A controller is a class in `server/controllers/` that answers HTTP requests. `RequestRoute` on the class gives its path, and `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` says who may call it. `GetRoute`, `PostRoute` and the other route annotations mark the methods that answer. Each method name starts with its verb, such as `getProducts`. A returned model, or a list of models, becomes JSON with the model's field names. `ResponseStatus(201)` sets the status code. `FromBody` reads the JSON body into a model (a data type in `server/models/`). A body that does not fit the model gets 400 before the method runs. To set the status, headers and body yourself, answer with the language's own response: a Fetch `Response` in JavaScript and TypeScript, an `(HTTPStatus, headers, body)` tuple in Python, a `[status, headers, body]` array in Ruby, `http_response_code()`, `header()` and `echo` in PHP, the same `HttpExchange` in Java and Kotlin, `HttpResponseMessage` in C#, `http::Response` in Rust, a shelf `Response` in Dart and `*http.Response` in Go. If you return `text/html` yourself, Yon passes it through unchanged. Yon never renders it. A controller needs no framework import, base class, registration call or package.

features.title: Relaying to Ruby and other programs
features.summary: Yon supports controllers in many languages. A route method can return `relay(command, request)` to call another program that implements Handler Protocol v1. `request` is the method parameter without a marker. It is the request in the language's own type, and `relay` answers with the language's own response. In PHP, `Yon::relay(command)` forwards the current request. The application gives the command at the call site. Tachyon supervises the program. It limits the program to the time left in the request and to the process limits. features.title: Streaming controllers
features.summary: StreamRoute marks a controller method that answers GET requests with a stream of server-sent events (SSE). The method produces many values, one at a time, with the language's own `yield` syntax, and its name starts with `stream`. It keeps the loop in a private generator method and only passes on that method's values. Tachyon sends each value as one limited event, and an end event when the method finishes. In the browser, StreamRequest on an HTTPClient method receives the stream. Tachyon opens it when a component first uses the client, reconnects with a growing wait (at most five tries), and closes it with the component. Each message is checked against the model type of the method's one parameter, passed to the method, and published as that model's event, so an OnEvent listener in any Tac language receives it. Java, Rust and Go cannot stream, because they have no native generator. Like every route, a stream says who may call it with `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`.

features.title: Socket controllers
features.summary: SocketRoute marks a controller class that keeps a WebSocket open, as Jakarta's @ServerEndpoint does. Tachyon makes one object of the class for each connection, so its fields hold that connection's state. OnOpen, OnMessage, OnClose and OnError mark the methods that run when a browser connects, sends a message, leaves, or when a method fails. Each message is JSON text, and Tachyon checks it against the model type of the OnMessage parameter first. The session sends messages back, and openSessions() (open_sessions() in Python, Ruby and Rust, OpenSessions() in Go, C# and F#, getOpenSessions() in Java) returns every open connection of the same path, so one message can go to every tab. When OnOpen or OnMessage fails, OnError runs and the socket stays open, as in Jakarta. In the browser, SocketRequest on an HTTPClient method receives the messages and publishes each one as its model's event, and the client's send(message) writes to the socket. Sockets are written in any Yon language. `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the class says who may connect; Tachyon answers 401 or 403 before it opens the socket.

features.title: Ordinary application modules
features.summary: Controllers use ordinary application helpers. The helpers need no registration and no required role names. Annotated controllers and providers must follow strict rules: role suffixes (fixed name endings), exact file names and plural folders. Tachyon finds them in the shared role folders of the realm (Tac or Yon). It combines the files in the same language into one checked annotation unit. Discovery does not scan at run time. It does not create global dependency injection (one shared system that gives every class the objects it needs). The helpers shown here have no annotations. They follow the usual composition rules of their language. Plain helpers belong in server/shared/. Tachyon does not treat them as framework roles. When you need automatic composition, use the normal imports of the language or the managed role examples. A Go file in server/shared/ is another file of the package main of the controller. So Go code calls it without an import. A controller file contains only its controller class and its imports.

features.title: Compiled services publish to the page
features.summary: Native services, WebAssembly services and TypeScript or Dart browser services inject an `ApplicationEventPublisher` for local events. `OnEvent` receives the events, and `OnStart`/`OnStop` run when the service starts and stops. Call the publisher to publish an event. A listener that is not `InBackground` can also return a model value. The runtime then publishes it as the model named by the return type of the listener. Each activation gets a new ID. The runtime rejects callbacks from an old activation. Each example publishes a `CatalogCount` model when it starts and updates its count in a listener for that model. Ruby names the model of a listener in a YARD tag, # @param value [CatalogCount]. The JavaScript `CatalogService` only listens, to events published by its native or WebAssembly counterpart.

class CatalogService
  # @return [Integer]
  attr_reader :count

  def initialize
    @count = 0
    @events = ApplicationEventPublisher.new
  end

  # @return [void]
  #[OnStart]
  def initialize_count
    announce
  end

  # @param value [CatalogCount]
  # @return [void]
  #[OnEvent]
  def changed(value)
    @count = value.count
  end

  # @return [void]
  #[OnStop]
  def cleanup
    @count = 0
  end

  private

  # @return [void]
  def announce
    @events.publish_event(CatalogCount.new(count: 5))
  end
end

features.title: Configuration as data
features.summary: `client/manifest.json` is the whole Tac configuration (ADR 0052). Its standard members name the application, choose the page it opens at and list its icons. Its `tac` member holds the application identity and window, page metadata, shared browser assets, service-worker cache rules and the sitemap settings. It is data, so every build reads it the same way without running code. The whole file is sent to the browser, so never put a secret in it. `tac.outgoing.hosts` lists the hosts that page code may call; the build and the page's security policy refuse the others. The file is public, so the build refuses a secret in it (`TY1324`).

features.title: Toolchain checks
features.summary: `ty doctor` checks whether this machine can build and run the project. It reports only the toolchains (compilers and build tools) and controller runtimes that the project uses. `--json` prints the same report in a format for other programs. A Rust, Go or C# service with no browser script also needs a WebAssembly check: `wasm32-unknown-unknown` for Rust, Go 1.27 for Go, or the .NET `wasm-tools` workload for C#. A Ruby service needs the tools that build Tachyon's Ruby WebAssembly runtime once: Ruby, Emscripten 6.0.10 or newer (`emcc`) and a C compiler. When the runtime is already in the Tachyon cache, the report shows it as ready instead. Each check has its own time limit: 10 seconds, and 60 seconds for the C# check, because it builds a small project. So a busy machine does not report a working toolchain as broken. The development server and `ty test` run the same checks before they start.

features.title: Hot updates while you edit
features.summary: A hot update changes the open page while you edit. A stylesheet update keeps the page state. A supported service update stops the service and starts it again. The service gets back the state that it chooses to keep. Only JavaScript and TypeScript services get hot updates. A change to a service in another language reloads the page, and the service starts again with its first values. Other changes can need a full page reload. A failed build keeps the last good page and shows a diagnostic overlay (error messages on top of the page) with the file, the line and help. The preview never stops because of a problem in your files: a project that is broken at start gets an error page until a save fixes it.

Window controls a desktop page may be granted

features.title: Request isolation
features.summary: By default, each request runs in one process with limits. With `YON_ISOLATION=firecracker`, Yon sends each supported request to a microVM control program. The deployment owns this program. A microVM is a small virtual machine. For now, this transport supports only JavaScript and Python controllers. A controller in another language fails before the driver starts. The handler protocol and the build do not change. Tachyon does not include the microVM program. It also does not yet claim that any microVM setup isolates requests safely.

files.name: isolation
files.code:
How a handler runs

  YON_ISOLATION=process       one supervised child process per
                              request. The default.

  YON_ISOLATION=firecracker   hand each request to a Firecracker
                              control program instead.

    YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER      the control program to run
    YON_FIRECRACKER_POOL        how many microVMs to keep
    YON_FIRECRACKER_VCPUS       vCPUs per microVM
    YON_FIRECRACKER_MEMORY_MIB  memory per microVM
    YON_FIRECRACKER_EGRESS      what a handler may reach

Read from the environment rather than a config file, because
which isolation a deployment wants is a property of where it
runs, not of the source — the same build runs either way.

An invalid or half-declared policy fails as TY2010 before a
handler runs, rather than falling back to something weaker than
what was asked for.

features.title: Serving what was published
features.summary: `ty start` serves a bundle that is already built. `server/application.json` and its profile files hold `yon` settings that are not secret. These files have no `yon` root key (top-level key). `.env` holds private Yon secrets. Public `tac` settings are already in the bundle. The deployment chooses the runtime executable and the isolation policy. `outgoing.hosts` in `server/application.json` lists the hosts that Yon code may call; at run time a local guard refuses every other host.

features.title: What a project looks like
features.summary: A project has two directories: `client` and `server`. HTTPClient routes contain a `tac.html` file. Server controllers live in `server/controllers`, and their annotations give the routes. HTTPClient behavior is in service classes under `client/services`. Application helpers are ordinary code in their language. Role types for `Allow`, such as `Admin`, are empty classes in `server/roles`, and the one `IdentityProvider` class lives in `server/controllers`.

What `ty init` lays out

  client/
    pages/        one directory per route, holding a tac.html
    components/   a two-level path, <product-card>: a view and its styles
    services/     one <Name>Service class per file, addressed as {name.field}
    clients/      collaborators a service injects; also stores/,

    models/       data types in TypeScript, Rust, C#, Dart, Kotlin or Swift,
                  never shipped on their own
    tests/        <Name>Test files run by ty test
    shared/       published as-is, imported by both halves

  server/
    routes/       yon.* files exposing the fixed Handler type
    services/     optional ordinary application modules
    stores/       optional ordinary application modules
    clients/      optional ordinary application modules
    helpers/      optional helper classes, and programs reached with
                  relay(...) or a @Gateway command
    models/       data types in TypeScript, Rust, C#, Dart, Kotlin, Java,
                  Python or PHP
    tests/        <Name>Test files run by ty test
    vendor/       third-party code, checked in
    config/       configuration a handler reads
    data/         files a handler reads or writes
    gateways/     reserved: Tachyon generates @Gateway units here, never
                  author files in it

  client/manifest.json   name, icons, start_url, and in tac: the
                        application identity and window, metadata,
                        shared assets, cache rules and the sitemap

tac.html, client/services and yon.* Handler entry points are framework
contracts, and so are the plural role folders: a role-annotated type is
discovered by the folder it sits in and the filename matching its type
(ADR 0031). models/ holds data types only (ADR 0041, ADR 0043), and
tests/ is where ty test looks. The remaining names are starter
conventions and can be changed or omitted.
